quizzes.stem: A marketing manager who configures Projects and drafts campaign material daily, and has never written code, wants a Claude certification. Which choice fits best?

options.a: The one for senior architects who govern enterprise solutions end to end
options.b: The one for engineers who build products with interfaces and protocols
options.c: The one for architects who design agentic production systems for customers
options.d: The one for business users applying the assistant to routine work

explanation.d: The Associate is for professionals who use Claude as a productivity tool, and it needs no software-development experience (the table and the choosing section).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the Developer row is for "Engineers who build with the API, Claude Code and MCP", which describes someone writing code.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the Architect, Foundations row is for "Solution architects who build production applications with Claude".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the Professional exam is for "Mid to senior architects who design, build and govern production solutions".

quizzes.stem: A candidate scores 760 overall but only 55 percent in one domain, and asks whether she passed. What is the correct reading?

options.a: Yes: the combined scaled figure alone decides the outcome
options.b: No, because every single domain needs a minimum share of correct items
options.c: No, she must retake only that domain after a short waiting period
options.d: Neither yet, since the result is withheld until a reviewer weighs each domain

explanation.a: The page says the domain percentages "are there to guide revision and are not used to decide pass or fail, which depends on the total scaled score".
explanation.b: Ruled out because pass or fail "depends on the total scaled score", with no per-domain minimum.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the "percentages are there to guide revision and are not used to decide pass or fail", and the page describes no domain-only retake.
explanation.d: Ruled out because you get "pass or fail, your scaled score, and the percentage correct in each domain", with nothing withheld for a review.

quizzes.stem: A candidate plans to prepare by collecting live test items that others have posted online. What is the best advice?

options.a: Use them only for the domains that carry the heaviest weights in the guide
options.b: Use them, since repeated questions are the surest route to a pass mark
options.c: Avoid them: that material is confidential and the skill is judgment
options.d: Share them with colleagues so that everyone benefits equally from the effort

explanation.c: The content is confidential, and "the skill is reasoning about the situation".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Studying for a memorised answer" is the trap named, and the questions are scenarios.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the "questions, options and scenarios are Anthropic's confidential property", whatever the domain.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "you accept a non-disclosure agreement before the exam begins", and passing the questions on breaks it.

quizzes.stem: A candidate with a documented condition needing extra time books her exam for Friday and asks for the adjustment on Thursday. What is the problem?

options.a: Adjustments are only ever given for test-centre sittings, and never for online ones
options.b: Approval has to come first, and the appointment should have followed it
options.c: The adjustment needs a second payment made on the same day as the request
options.d: Extra time is added automatically for anyone who simply asks on the day itself

explanation.b: The fixed order is to request through the test provider, wait for approval and only then schedule.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page says accommodations are for "documented disabilities or needs", with no restriction by delivery mode.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page describes no extra payment, only "request the accommodation through Pearson VUE, wait for approval, and only then schedule the exam".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Extra time or a break you did not arrange in advance is not available on the day".

quizzes.stem: A candidate registered under a nickname, but her passport shows her full legal name. What should she do?

options.a: Use a second photo card that carries her nickname
options.b: Bring a letter from her employer explaining the nickname on the day
options.c: Plan to explain the difference to the proctor when she sits down to start
options.d: Have the entry amended through the support contact before booking a slot

explanation.d: The name must match exactly, and a correction is made before scheduling through the support contact in the guide.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "The name on your registration must match your ID exactly", and an employer's letter is not an accepted fix.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "if the name differs, you may be refused entry and lose the fee", so nothing can be explained away at check-in.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the ID must be "a valid, unexpired, government-issued photo ID", and a card showing a nickname is not one.

quizzes.stem: A candidate's credential ran out three weeks ago, and she hopes to use the free renewal assessment. What is the accurate position?

options.a: She can still take the free assessment within a grace period of about a month
options.b: That step had to happen earlier, so she needs the whole exam again
options.c: She pays half the usual fee and sits a shortened version of the test
options.d: She keeps the badge on display and simply updates the date on her profile

explanation.b: Renewal is before expiry, and "after a lapse the full exam is needed" at the full fee.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the Exam Policy says "once a certification has expired you can no longer renew it".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the lapsed holder "must retake the full exam at the full fee".
explanation.d: Ruled out because under the Terms "you must not present yourself as currently certified after it expires".

quizzes.stem: A scenario describes a manager asking Claude to summarise a regulation, with a clause cited. Among the options is one that has the assistant rate its own certainty. Which distractor family is this?

options.a: Self-verification, where the model vouches for itself
options.b: Too much machinery, meaning a heavy build for a simple problem
options.c: A different problem, meaning a real fix aimed at the wrong target
options.d: Right idea, wrong moment, meaning a correct step taken too late

explanation.a: The table gives "Asks the model to confirm itself" as the self-verification family, with "Ask Claude how confident it is" as its sound.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Too much machinery" means "Solves a simple problem with a heavy build", and a request for a rating builds nothing.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A different problem" is one that "Fixes something real that is not the one described", while this option targets the real problem with a weak method.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Right idea, wrong moment" is a "Correct step done too early, too late or out of order", and a self-rating is not a correct step at any time.

quizzes.stem: A candidate spends several minutes going over the whole scenario twice before locating the question sentence, and then runs short of time. Which step of the working method was skipped?

options.a: Begin with the ask itself, then take in the situation with that in mind
options.b: Form a one-line answer only after reading every option in turn
options.c: Change an answer only after spotting a new fact in the text
options.d: Count the answers to select just before submitting the item

explanation.a: The first step of the method is "Read the ask first", then the situation is read with it in mind.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the method says "Form a one-line answer, then look for it", so the prediction comes before the options and not after them.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A new fact you noticed is a reason; a feeling is not" concerns revising an answer, not the order of reading.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the step reads "Check it again before you submit", which comes at the end and does not explain time lost at the start.

quizzes.stem: With three weeks left, a candidate misses most mock questions on one heavily weighted topic area. Which plan fits the page?

options.a: Skip it, because pass or fail ignores results by area
options.b: Memorise the mock's answers, since the real exam repeats them
options.c: Study that block first, and practise it on a spaced schedule
options.d: Take the mock again at once, hoping the result improves

explanation.c: The plan is to study the weakest domains first and work the review bank for them on the spaced schedule.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the mock's job is to "Test readiness under time, and find weak domains", not to be learned by heart.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the plan says to "Study the weakest domains first, weighted by their share of the exam".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the plan says to "Take the mock exam once, untimed, and mark each miss with its domain and the reason" before any second attempt.

quizzes.stem: A candidate with a documented need for extra time wants to sit the Architect Foundations exam. She books a slot first, then requests the adjustment. Which statement is accurate?

options.a: The slot is fine, since adjustments are granted on the day itself
options.b: Approval had to come before the appointment was made
options.c: Approval is unnecessary, as a proctor can add time whenever asked
options.d: The adjustment can be made only at a test centre, forcing a rebooking

explanation.b: The fixed order is to request the accommodation and wait for approval before scheduling.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Extra time or a break you did not arrange in advance is not available on the day".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "an unapproved break counts as misconduct", so a proctor cannot add time on request.
explanation.d: Ruled out because accommodations are for "documented disabilities or needs, in line with applicable law", with no limit to test centres.

quizzes.stem: A score report shows 80 percent in one domain, 40 percent in another and a scaled score of 700. What should the candidate conclude?

options.a: A fail, and a retake can happen the very next day at no extra cost
options.b: A pass, because the strong section outweighs the weak one
options.c: A fail, as the pass mark is 720; study the weak area first
options.d: Borderline, so a reviewer will re-score the weakest section by hand

explanation.c: The pass mark is a scaled score of 720, so 700 fails, and the sensible reaction is to use the domain figures to aim revision.
explanation.b: Ruled out because pass or fail "depends on the total scaled score", not on the stronger domain.
explanation.a: Ruled out because retake waits are "14 days after the first, 30 days after the second", and each attempt costs the full fee.
explanation.d: Ruled out because you get "pass or fail, your scaled score, and the percentage correct in each domain", with no review of a score by hand.

quizzes.stem: On a 60-item sitting of 120 minutes, a candidate spends five minutes on each of the first twenty items. What follows?

options.a: She should rush the first items instead, since early items carry most weight
options.b: Nothing, because unanswered items are not scored against her
options.c: The proctor pauses the clock, since the sitting allows extra minutes on hard items
options.d: Only about thirty seconds per remaining question is left, so she must speed up

explanation.d: Twenty items at five minutes use 100 of the 120 minutes, leaving 20 minutes for 40 items.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the page says to "leave no item blank by choice", since no penalty for a wrong answer is described.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the exam is "120 minutes of exam time", a fixed limit.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the sensible pattern is "answering what you know and keeping a note of the uncertain ones", not rushing the start.

quizzes.stem: A candidate plans to take timed mocks only, one per week, and to learn the exam software the night before. Which change fits the page best?

options.a: Drop the mocks entirely, since the real items will differ in any case
options.b: Review missed topics on a spaced schedule, and study the interface well ahead
options.c: Cram everything into the final weekend, when memory is freshest
options.d: Take two mocks in one day, so that the score settles sooner

explanation.b: The routine pairs spaced practice on misses with learning the interface from the provider's tutorial, well before the day.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the mock exists to "Test readiness under time, and find weak domains".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Spaced practice over weeks does more than one long session".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Short daily sessions beat long weekend ones", and two mocks in a day is a long session.

quizzes.stem: A user pastes a 25-page report beneath a one-line question and gets weak, unfocused answers. Which change is most likely to help?

options.a: Add a role such as world-class analyst to sharpen the focus
options.b: Shorten the question to a single word so that it stands out
options.c: Ask Claude to read the pasted pages twice before replying
options.d: Put the long material at the top, and the ask at the very end

explanation.d: Long inputs go near the top with the query at the end (module 6, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the guidance is to "Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query", not to shorten the question.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Hiding the task in the middle" is the trap, and rereading does not move the task.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential", so it changes voice and not focus on the material.

quizzes.stem: A prompt supplies four policy documents, and the answers never say which document backs each claim, so reviewers cannot trace them. Which change fits best?

options.a: Merge the four into one paragraph so that they read smoothly
options.b: Wrap each in a numbered tagged block and ask for the number cited
options.c: Tell Claude to cite its sources more carefully in general
options.d: Rename the tags with something creative for each policy

explanation.b: Nested tagged blocks with an index let the answer name the one it used (module 6, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the guidance is to nest "each with an index or a name", the opposite of merging.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the guidance is to "Refer to tags by name in the instructions", which a general plea does not do.
explanation.d: Ruled out because tag names "have to be meaningful and used the same way every time".

quizzes.stem: A team needs replies in a rarely seen house format of three labelled lines, and instructions alone give inconsistent layouts. Which prompting style fits best?

options.a: Multi-shot, with a few varied samples of the wanted shape
options.b: Zero-shot, with a longer written description of the format
options.c: One-shot, with a sample taken from an unrelated task
options.d: No samples, with a role line promising to follow the layout

explanation.a: A rare format with subtle boundaries calls for several varied examples (module 6, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because zero-shot suits a case where "The task is common and easy to describe", and this format is not.
explanation.c: Ruled out because examples should "Mirror your actual use case closely", and an unrelated sample does not.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential", so a role line does not fix a layout.

quizzes.stem: A manager types "Write something about our Q3 results" and receives a generic paragraph with no figures. Which revision best fixes the request?

options.a: Name the readers, the form, the numbers, and how to handle gaps
options.b: Ask for a longer piece, since more words will carry more detail
options.c: Add a reassuring role such as senior analyst, and keep the rest as it is
options.d: Run it several times and pick whichever result sounds best

explanation.a: A good description gives the product, the process and the performance, with the goal and context.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Describing the topic, not the job" is the trap, and length adds no audience or form.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential", so a role does not supply missing figures.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method".

quizzes.stem: A knowledge-base assistant answers every question, even when the manuals say nothing, and sometimes invents a procedure. Which prompt addition best tackles this?

options.a: Add the manuals to every request, even when they are unrelated
options.b: Raise the temperature so that it explores more possible answers
options.c: Allow it to admit that the supplied material does not address the matter
options.d: Ask for a confidence percentage beside each answer it gives

explanation.c: Permission to say the material is insufficient is the first listed technique (module 1, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Higher temperatures lead to more creative and diverse outputs", which invites invention.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "more context isn't automatically better", and unrelated manuals dilute the relevant ones.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "asking a model how sure it is does not make a wrong answer right".

quizzes.stem: A test asserts that a Claude reply matches a stored string exactly. It passes today and fails tomorrow for the same input. What is the best interpretation?

options.a: The vendor swapped the model silently, so the id must be pinned and re-recorded
options.b: Replies can vary even at fixed settings, so judge quality across many cases
options.c: The prompt is faulty, and a line such as be consistent will stabilise it
options.d: The machine's clock changed the output, so the time must be frozen

explanation.b: Output varies by sampling and infrastructure, so one run proves nothing (module 1, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because every id is pinned, "including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A prompt sentence does not remove sampling".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "The model has no clock", so freezing one changes nothing.

quizzes.stem: A clinic administrator plans to have Claude read radiology scans uploaded by patients and report findings to them directly. Which concern matters most?

options.a: Names of the people in the images would be read out and shared automatically
options.b: Claude cannot read any image, so every scan would have to be described in words first
options.c: The scans are fine for the purpose, provided that they are sharp and in colour
options.d: These images lie outside the design, and a qualified reviewer must vet outputs

explanation.d: The vision limits include scans, and a decision reaching individuals needs a qualified reviewer (modules 4 and 10).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Claude reads images and PDFs".
explanation.c: Ruled out because Claude is "not designed to interpret complex diagnostic scans such as CTs or MRIs", whatever the image quality.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Claude cannot be used to name people in images, and refuses to".

quizzes.stem: A communications assistant drafts a press note with Claude. It contains a quotation attributed to the chief executive and three statistics, and time is short. What should be checked first?

options.a: Spelling and tone, since those errors are the most visible
options.b: The CEO's remark and the figures, against the originals
options.c: Whether Claude says it is confident about each claim
options.d: Whether a second Claude draft contains the same claims

explanation.b: The claims that would hurt if wrong are checked against the source of record (module 5, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible, and skip figures and citations, which are where the damage is".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the routine is "Check those against the source of record, not against the model".

quizzes.stem: An analyst needs Claude's output to load into a database through a script, and also to show executives a short takeaway. Which pair of formats fits?

options.a: A published artifact with shared storage serving both audiences
options.b: An artifact for the ingest step, and a table in a slide deck for leadership
options.c: Inline replies for both, since artifacts only suit code
options.d: Machine-readable results for the ingest step, a brief inline note for leadership

explanation.d: Data a program reads is structured data, and a short takeaway stays inline (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Data that another program will read is structured data", not an artifact.
explanation.c: Ruled out because an artifact suits "A document, deck, dashboard or small tool to hand to someone", not only code.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the warning is to "check whether the artifact uses shared storage" before sensitive entries.

quizzes.stem: A long Claude summary says in its first paragraph that revenue grew eight percent, and in its fifth that revenue declined slightly. What is the best step?

options.a: Check both statements against the source, then correct the draft
options.b: Keep the paragraph that appears first, since earlier text is more reliable
options.c: Ask Claude to reconcile the two and trust its reconciled text
options.d: Average the two figures to estimate the true growth

explanation.a: A contradiction is a signal to check the source of record (module 5, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Confidence of tone is not a signal", and position is no better.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the routine is "Check those against the source of record, not against the model".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "the careless move is to fill the gap with an estimate".

quizzes.stem: A retailer will draft about 5,000 short order-status replies an hour. Speed and cost matter most, and the replies are routine. What is the best starting point?

options.a: Use the middle tier until the invoices arrive, then decide
options.b: Use the most capable tier for every reply to protect quality
options.c: Begin with the fast, inexpensive tier and test it on past cases
options.d: Pick whichever tier the most experienced colleague prefers

explanation.c: High-volume routine work starts on the efficient tier and is validated on real data (module 3, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "the top tier for everything wastes the budget".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the decision rule is to "build benchmark tests for your use case", not wait for invoices.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Having a good evaluation set is the most important step", which preference is not.

quizzes.stem: A long chat in the app starts contradicting earlier decisions after many hours, though no error appears. What is the best action?

options.a: Instruct Claude to delete the older turns from its memory
options.b: Keep going, since a larger window guarantees consistent recall
options.c: Begin anew with a short recap of what was agreed
options.d: Upgrade to a model with a bigger window and carry on regardless

explanation.c: A fresh start with a summary keeps the useful context and drops the rot (module 1, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because of the trap "Reading the window size as a promise of quality".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "what looks like learning inside one conversation is the context window doing its job", so Claude cannot delete memory on request.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Larger windows raise the ceiling; they do not remove the need to decide what goes in".

quizzes.stem: A strategist must compare twelve vendors using public sources and wants cited findings by tomorrow, with several rounds of investigation expected. Which feature fits best?

options.a: Research mode, with the web lookup setting enabled
options.b: A Project holding the vendors' brochures and no web access
options.c: A plain chat reply, since citations arrive with every answer
options.d: An artifact that renders the comparison as a dashboard first

explanation.a: Research runs many linked searches with citations and needs web search on (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because a Project suits "Recurring work with fixed rules and reference files".
explanation.c: Ruled out because plain chat is for "A one-off question, a draft, a quick comparison".
explanation.d: Ruled out because an artifact is for "A document, deck, dashboard or small tool to hand to someone", not for gathering sources.

quizzes.stem: A user tells Claude about her project in an incognito chat and finds that the next chat has no trace of it. Is this a fault?

options.a: No: she should have used a Project, since Projects always remember everything
options.b: Yes: the weights should have updated after the conversation
options.c: Yes: memory failed because the conversation was too short
options.d: No: such conversations are kept out of memory and history by design

explanation.d: Incognito chats are kept out of memory and history on purpose (modules 7 and 10).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Weights are fixed at inference time".
explanation.c: Ruled out because incognito chats "keep a conversation out of memory and history", so memory did not fail.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Each project has its own separate memory space and dedicated project summary", and a Project does not remember everything.

quizzes.stem: A COO asks which of four chores suit Claude with review: (1) drafting vendor-email variants, (2) deciding which supplier to drop, (3) summarising call transcripts, (4) calculating invoice totals. Which pair is right?

options.a: The second and fourth
options.b: The first and third
options.c: The third and fourth
options.d: The first and second

explanation.b: Chore 1 and chore 3 are language-shaped work that a review can catch, while the supplier decision and exact sums are not (module 5, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because chore 2 needs "judgment that carries accountability", and chore 4 needs exactness.
explanation.c: Ruled out because chore 4, the totals, needs "exactness (money, counts, identifiers)".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "A step stays with a person, or with code" when it needs accountable judgment such as the supplier decision in chore 2.

quizzes.stem: A department head asks how Claude will change the team's work. Which message is the most balanced?

options.a: It cannot be trusted at all, so every use must be forbidden until further notice
options.b: It will do the job on its own, so we can cut the review time right away
options.c: It speeds drafts and summaries, people still check claims, results get measured
options.d: It is just a faster search engine, so nothing about anyone's role will change

explanation.c: A fair message states what it speeds up, what still needs a person and how the team will know it works (module 5, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the message should say "what still needs a person (checking claims, decisions, anything regulated)".
explanation.a: Ruled out because it must include "how you will know it works (a spot-check rate, an example set, a before and after on time)", not a ban.
explanation.d: Ruled out because it ignores "what it speeds up (first drafts, summaries, comparisons, variations)".

quizzes.stem: An FP&A analyst must trace how a revenue figure in a long workbook is derived before presenting it. Which capability of the Excel add-in helps most directly?

options.a: Reading closed workbooks stored in the shared drive
options.b: Automatic sign-off of the figure by the add-in once it is asked
options.c: Macro execution that recalculates the whole workbook automatically
options.d: Answers about the open file that carry cell-level citations

explanation.d: The add-in answers with clickable cell-level citations (module 8, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because it is "Not recommended for final client deliverables without human review".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Claude can read and write only files that are open at that moment".

quizzes.stem: A grants officer has Claude draft a funder report saying the programme transformed the community, with percentages taken from last year's file. Which review matters most?

options.a: Polish the wording so that the funder finds it persuasive
options.b: Tie each stated outcome and ratio back to the organisation's own data
options.c: Ask Claude to estimate how likely each percentage is to be correct
options.d: Remove all percentages so that no figure can be wrong

explanation.b: Impact claims and statistics are checked against the source (module 9, page 2).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the hidden risk is "Overstating results to a funder", which polish worsens.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the check is "every claim about impact, every statistic and every funder requirement against the source".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the check that matters most is "Impact claims and statistics against source", not their removal.

quizzes.stem: An online shop wants every order with a postcode outside its delivery zones flagged automatically, and 12,000 orders arrive daily. Which design is best?

options.a: A short program applies the geographic rule; Claude drafts customer notes
options.b: Claude reads each order and decides whether the postcode lies out of zone
options.c: Claude checks a sample of orders and the rest are assumed to be fine
options.d: Claude flags suspicious postcodes by feel, then code confirms them

explanation.a: A rule that fits in one line belongs in code (module 4, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because code is "Cheaper, faster, deterministic, testable".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A prompt is a request, not a guarantee", and a sample leaves the rest unchecked.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "If you can write the rule, write it; add a model only for the cases the rule cannot express".

quizzes.stem: A coordinator builds a small published artifact where visitors enter their dietary needs, and it keeps data. What should she check before inviting people?

options.a: Whether its storage is personal or visible to every user
options.b: Whether the artifact runs past fifteen lines, which decides its storage
options.c: Whether each visitor has the creator's plan, as usage bills to it
options.d: Whether visitors have connected the creator's own apps

explanation.a: Shared storage is visible to every user, so check it before sensitive entries (module 7, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the fifteen-line figure is about when an artifact is made, "typically over 15 lines, and reusable on its own".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Their use counts against their own plan limits, not the creator's".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "each person connects their own apps even in a shared artifact".

quizzes.stem: A Project's HR assistant quotes a leave policy that was replaced, and both the old and the new document sit in its knowledge. What is the best fix?

options.a: Ask Claude to merge both files into a third file
options.b: Add an instruction to prefer the newer document whenever they conflict
options.c: Delete the superseded file and keep a copy in your own storage
options.d: Switch on memory so that Claude learns which policy is current

explanation.c: A deleted file is a guarantee, and the old copy is kept in your own storage (module 7, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "an instruction is a request and a deleted file is a guarantee".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Judge the source before you add it", and a merged file adds a new unchecked source.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "memory is not a substitute for a knowledge file".

quizzes.stem: A team lead wants to share a Project that holds salary bands with the whole organisation. Which approach is right?

options.a: Rely on the instructions to keep the salary files hidden from the viewers
options.b: Grant it only to people entitled to the knowledge, since viewing shows everything
options.c: Share it widely, because can-view access stops viewers from reading the knowledge
options.d: Share it with everyone first and delete the files later if that proves necessary

explanation.b: Sharing shows the instructions and every file to everyone with access (module 7, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the guidance is "Treat sharing as publishing".
explanation.c: Ruled out because can-view gives "read-only access to contents, knowledge and instructions", which is reading.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "anyone with access can read the instructions and every file in the knowledge base", and deleting later does not undo that.

quizzes.stem: A team wants every Claude Tag reply in one Slack channel to be brief and to link its source. How should the lead set this up?

options.a: Edit the model's settings so that its temperature drops to a lower value
options.b: Ask each member to type the rule again in every single thread they open
options.c: Set it in a Project, because Slack reads the Project's own instructions first
options.d: Tell the assistant so right there, where it is saved as standing instructions

explanation.d: Standing instructions are set by telling Claude in the channel, and they go to channel memory (module 8, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "they go to channel memory, which admins can review and delete", so members need not repeat them.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Project instructions apply to every chat in that Project", not to Slack.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them", so a temperature setting is not available.

quizzes.stem: A researcher wants Claude to analyse survey responses that include names and a free-text notes column. Which preparation is best?

options.a: Delete only the name column, since notes cannot identify anyone
options.b: Aggregate or generalise, and scan open-ended comments for stray details
options.c: Replace names with codes and keep the key file beside the data
options.d: Upload everything and ask for a summary that omits personal details

explanation.b: Aggregate or generalise, and check free-text columns, which hide details (module 10, page 1).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Notes columns hide names and details".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Pseudonymised data is still personal data under many rules, because the key can reverse it".
explanation.d: Ruled out because asking for a summary without personal details "is a request, and it does not satisfy a policy control".

quizzes.stem: A professional asks Claude in Chrome to shortlist conference venues while her banking site is open in another tab. Which habit best limits harm?

options.a: Trust the classifier, since the risk of an attack is nil
options.b: Leave the bank tab open but tell Claude to ignore it
options.c: Switch on Skip all approvals so that no prompt interrupts the task
options.d: Use a clean profile, and approve each action manually

explanation.d: A separate profile and manual approval limit what Claude can see and do (module 8, page 2).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "whatever is visible in them becomes part of the conversation".
explanation.c: Ruled out because in that mode "Claude does not pause and nothing checks its actions".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the page says plainly that "the risk is not zero".

quizzes.stem: A consultant on a Pro plan asks whether her chats may be used to improve Claude. What is the accurate answer?

options.a: Only if she has allowed it in her settings, and incognito sessions are excluded
options.b: Always, since consumer plans train on every single conversation they hold
options.c: Never, under any circumstance, even when she presses the feedback buttons
options.d: Only for the first thirty days after each conversation has taken place

explanation.a: Consumer chats improve Claude only by choice, and incognito chats are excluded (module 10, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because chats are used "only if you choose to allow it in your privacy settings".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Giving feedback with the thumbs buttons stores the conversation for up to five years".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "where it is off, a deleted chat leaves the back end within 30 days", which is not a window on use.

quizzes.stem: A manager lets Cowork reach her entire documents drive to save time, and it holds tax returns and exported passwords. What should change?

options.a: Keep the access and rely on the cloud sandbox to protect everything
options.b: Keep the access but switch to automatic approval for speed
options.c: Connect a dedicated folder containing only the task's files
options.d: Keep the access, but ask Claude to ignore the sensitive files

explanation.c: A dedicated working folder limits what a mistake or an injected instruction can reach (module 8, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the habit is to "use Manual approval for sensitive files, new tools and hard-to-undo actions".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the isolation "doesn't limit what Claude reads or does" through connected tools.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the habit is to "grant access selectively and avoid financial documents, credentials and personal records".

quizzes.stem: A model gives correct, well-formatted answers on a labelling task but is too slow for a live chat widget, and the instructions and context are good. Which step fits?

options.a: Reword it with a stronger role such as expert labeller
options.b: Add more context to the prompt, since slowness comes from missing detail
options.c: Evaluate a faster tier or lower effort against the same test set
options.d: Add a retrieval step to supply today's data

explanation.c: Correct instructions and context with a speed miss point to another tier or lower effort, tested on the same set (module 6, page 4).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table describes this case as "Correct instructions, correct context, still a capability or speed miss".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "A role changes the voice, not the facts".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the table's fix for the wrong model is "Evaluate another tier or raise effort", and retrieval supplies missing facts.

quizzes.stem: A nightly job re-scores 200,000 archived documents, and the results are due the next morning. Which cost lever fits best?

options.a: Batched requests, which are half the price of standard ones
options.b: Prompt cache reads, which price every output token lower
options.c: Fast mode, which doubles the output speed at premium pricing
options.d: Higher effort, which trades latency for cost

explanation.a: Latency-tolerant bulk work suits batches, which are 50 percent cheaper (module 3, page 1).
explanation.b: Ruled out because cache reads are described as costing "a fraction of the base input price", and these documents are all different.
explanation.c: Ruled out because fast mode offers "up to 2.5x higher output speed at premium pricing", which raises cost.
explanation.d: Ruled out because effort "trades intelligence for latency and cost within a single model", not bulk cost.

quizzes.stem: After a mock, a candidate notices that most misses were options that asked Claude to confirm its own answer. What is the best next step?

options.a: Retake the mock at once, without reading the pages behind the misses
options.b: Memorise the answer letters for each such question in the bank
options.c: Ignore them, as the domain results do not decide the pass
options.d: Study that distractor family, and why claims go to the source

explanation.d: Study the family and the rule that confidence is not evidence (module 11, page 3).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Studying for a memorised answer" is the trap named.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the "percentages are there to guide revision", so a pattern in misses is a signal.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the plan is to "read the page behind every miss" before a second attempt.
